etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stele, stel, from Old English stīele, from Proto-West Germanic *stahlī (“something made of steel”), enlargement of *stahl (“steel”), from Proto-Germanic *stahlą, from *stah- or *stag- (“to be firm, rigid”), from Proto-Indo-European *stak- (“to stay, to be firm”). Compare Scots stele, Yola stehli.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) An artificial metal produced from iron, harder and more elastic than elemental iron; used figuratively as a symbol of hardness.

quote.citation: c. 725, Corpus Gloss., published 1431:
quote.text: Ocearium stæli.

quote.citation: c. 825, Epinal Gloss., section 49:
quote.text: Accearium steeli.

quote.citation: c. 1275, Laȝamon, Brut, 12916:
quote.text: Þe alle þine leomen wule to-draȝen. þeh þu weore stel al.

quote.citation: c. 1473, Raoul Le Fèvre, translated by William Caxton, The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, section I:
quote.text: Employeng the steell of his swerd the most best wyse that in hym was possible.

quote.citation: c. 1480, St. Mary Magdalen, 408 in 1896, W. M. Metcalfe, Legends Saints Sc. Dial., I 267:
quote.text: Weman...with wordis cane rycht wele our-cum mene hard as stele.

quote.citation: 1601, Pliny, translated by P. Holland, Hist. World, II xxxiv xiv 514:
quote.text: The purest part thereof [of iron ore] which in Latine is called Nucleus ferri, i. the kernell or heart of the yron (and it is that which we call steele)

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jeremiah 15:12:
quote.text: Shall yron breake the Northren yron, and the steele?(The Hebrew word is נחשת meaning copper. "Bow of steele" occurs in three places translating קשת נחושה.)

quote.citation: c. 1606–1607 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Anthonie and Cleopatra”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iv], line 33:
quote.text: ...Like a man of Steele.

quote.citation: 1839, A. Ure, Dict. Arts, published 1172:
quote.text: The bars are exposed to two or three successive processes of cementation, and are hence said to be twice or thrice converted into steels.

quote.citation: 1946, Thorpe's Dictionary of Applied Chemistry, 4th edition, VII 47 1:
quote.text: Steel may be roughly defined as an alloy of iron and carbon containing up to 1.7% carbon, all of the carbon being in the combined condition. A second definition, distinguishing it from cast or wrought iron, is that it has been produced in the molten condition, and a third states that steel can be hardened by quenching from a suitably high temperature. There are...certain exceptions to all these definitions.

quote.citation: 1976 Jul, Scientific American, 68 2:
quote.text: For the iron to be made into steel (defined as iron with a carefully controlled carbon content of 1.7 percent or less) the sulfur, the silicon, and the excess carbon must be removed.

definitions.definition: Bladed or pointed weapons, as swords, javelins, daggers.

quote.citation: c. 1250, The Owl & the Nightengale, published 1030:
quote.text: For heom ne may halter ne bridel Bringe from here wode wyse, Ne mon mid stele ne mid ire.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii], line 35:
quote.text: For braue Macbeth (well hee deſerues that Name)Diſdayning Fortune, with his brandiſht Steele,Which ſmoak'd with bloody execution(Like Valours Minion) caru'd out his paſſage.

quote.citation: 1712, Lord Shaftesbury, Characteristicks, III 115:
quote.text: But who wou'd dream that out of abundant Charity and Brotherly Love shou'd come Steel, Fire, Gibbets, Rods.

quote.citation: 1892, Rudyard Kipling, Barrack-room Ballads, section 139:
quote.text: They have asked for the steel. They shall have it now; Out cutlasses and board!

quote.text: While one man was beating off the swords, the waters stole up silently and took him. Contrariwise, another was struggling with the waves, when the steel came up and encompassed him. The flowing waters were befouled with the gory spray. Thus the Ruthenians were conquered...

definitions.definition: A piece used for striking sparks from flint.

quote.citation: c. 1220, Bestiary, section 535:
quote.text: Of ston mid stel in ðe tunder wel to brennen one ðis wunder.

quote.text: The Cock falling with its wonted violence upon the Steel.

definitions.definition: Armor.

quote.citation: c. 1330, Sir Tristrem, L 3324:

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv], page 33:

quote.citation: 1634 October 9 (first performance), [John Milton], edited by H[enry] Lawes, A Maske Presented at Ludlow Castle, 1634: […] [Comus], London:  […]  [Augustine Matthews] for Hvmphrey Robinson, […], published 1637, →OCLC; reprinted as Comus: […] (Dodd, Mead & Company’s Facsimile Reprints of Rare Books; Literature Series; no. I), New York, N.Y.: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1903, →OCLC, page 421:
quote.text: She that has [chastity], is clad in compleat steel.

definitions.definition: A honing steel, a tool used to sharpen or hone metal blades.

quote.citation: 1541 in 1844, J. Stuart, Extracts of the Council Register of Aberdeen, I 176:
quote.text: The steill to scherp the schawing jrne.

quote.citation: 1883, Howard Pyle, chapter V, in The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood […], New York, N.Y.:  […]  Charles Scribner’s Sons […], →OCLC:

quote.text: I haue a ruffe is a quarter deep, measured by the yeard... You haue a pretty set too, how big is the steele you set with?

quote.citation: 1904 February 22, Daily Chron, 5 4:
quote.text: I suppose the bullet must have struck the steels in my corsets.

definitions.definition: (dialectal) A flat iron.

quote.citation: 1638, J. Taylor, Bull, Beare, & Horse, C5:
quote.text: One of them having occasion to use a Steele, smoothing Iron, or some such kinde of Laundry Instrument.

definitions.definition: (sewing, dialectal) A sewing needle; a knitting needle; a sharp metal stylus.

quote.citation: 1785, William Cowper, Task, IV 165:

definitions.definition: (printing) An engraving plate:

quote.citation: 1887 June 11, Athenæum, 779 1:
quote.text: A re-issue of the Examples of the Architecture of Venice. By John Ruskin... With the Text, and the 16 Plates (10 Steels and 6 Lithographs) as originally published.

definitions.definition: Projectiles.

quote.citation: 1898 June 1, Westminster Gazette, 5 1:

definitions.definition: (sewing) A fringe of beads or decoration of this metal.

quote.citation: 1899 January 26, Daily News, 6 3:

definitions.definition: (music, guitar) A type of slide used while playing the steel guitar.
(countable) Any item made of this metal, particularly including:
(uncountable, medicine, obsolete) Medicinal consumption of this metal; chalybeate medicine; (eventually) any iron or iron-treated water consumed as a medical treatment.

quote.citation: 1649, H. Hammond, Christians Obligations, X 253:
quote.text: A stronger physick is now necessary, perhaps a whole course of steel: A physick, God knowes, that this Kingdome hath been under five or six yeares.

quote.citation: 1704, J. Harris, Lexicon Technicum, volume L:
quote.text: Steel is not so good as Iron for Medicinal Operation.

quote.citation: 1712 September 18, Journal to Stella, Jonathan Swift, II 558:
quote.text: The Doctor tells me I must go into a Course of Steel, tho I have not the Spleen.

quote.citation: 1866, Princess Alice, Mem., section 158:
quote.text: I...am really only kept alive by steel.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, colors) The gray hue of this metal; steel-gray, or steel blue.

quote.citation: 1851 Dec 28, E. Ruskin, letter in 1965, M. Lutyens, Effie in Venice, II 236:
quote.text: Falkenhayn gave...to Jane a steel glacé silk dress.

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, “Chapter 132”, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC:
quote.text: It was a clear steel-blue day. The firmaments of air and sea were hardly separable in that all-pervading azure; only, the pensive air was transparently pure and soft, with a woman’s look, and the robust and man-like sea heaved with long, strong, lingering swells, as Samson’s chest in his sleep.

definitions.definition: (figurative) Extreme hardness or resilience.
Made of steel.

quote.citation: mid-14th century, Alisaunder, 416:
quote.text: Strained in stel ger on steedes of might.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii], line 229:

quote.citation: 1976, J. Wheeler-Bennett, Friends, Enemies, & Sovereigns, V, 156:
quote.text: King Peter attributed his father's, King Alexander's, death to the fact that...he had not worn his steel-mesh bullet-proof shirt.

quote.citation: 1601, C[aius] Plinius Secundus [i.e., Pliny the Elder], “[Book VII.] LVI.”, in Philemon Holland, transl., The Historie of the World. Commonly Called, The Naturall Historie of C. Plinius Secundus. […], 1st tome, London:  […]  Adam Islip, →OCLC, page 188:

quote.citation: 1713 February 17, Journal to Stella, Jonathan Swift, II, 622:

definitions.definition: (printing) Engraved on steel.

quote.citation: 1880, Mark Twain, letter:

To steelify; to turn iron into steel.

definitions.definition: (literally) To treat or furnish with or transform into steel.
To harden or strengthen; to nerve or make obdurate; to fortify against.

quote.citation: 1581, Homer, translated by A. Hall, 10 Bks. Iliades, VI 110:
quote.text: But stil he was so steelde With heart so good, as victor he dead left them in the field.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i], line 148:

quote.citation: 1807, William Wordsworth, Sonn. to Liberty, II v:

definitions.definition: (figuratively) To cause to resemble steel.
(dialectal) To press with a flat iron.

quote.citation: 1746, Exmoor Scolding, 3rd edition, II 14:
quote.text: Tha hasn't tha Sense to stile thy own Dressing.
